fields.Back: A combination of attributes (or a single attribute) that can be used to enforce that no two tuples can be identical.

fields.Front: For the table SSN | LastName | FirstName (34 Simpson Homer; 56 Simpson Marge; 78 Smithers Marge; 99 Simpson Homer), what is the key?
fields.Back: Likely SSN alone (also SSN+FirstName, SSN+LastName, or all three). NOT LastName, FirstName, or LastName+FirstName (Simpson Homer appears twice).

fields.Front: A table LastName | FirstName with rows Simpson Homer, Simpson Marge, Smithers Marge, Simpson Homer: what is the key?
fields.Back: There is no key: rows 1 and 4 are identical, which Codd's model does not even allow. If the last row were Smithers Homer, (LastName, FirstName) could be a key in that snapshot, but the instructor calls it 'just a snapshot in time' and 'not a good key': the next Homer Smithers would break it.

fields.Front: Table Attribute1|Attribute2|Attribute3 with rows (a1,b1,c1),(a1,b2,c1),(a2,b1,c2),(a2,b2,c2): possible keys?
fields.Back: (Attribute1, Attribute2) or (Attribute2, Attribute3) or all three. No single attribute works; (Attribute1, Attribute3) fails because (a1,c1) repeats.

fields.Text: A superkey is {{c1::any}} set of attributes that enforces that no two tuples are alike.
A candidate key is a {{c1::minimal}} superkey: no {{c2::proper subset}} of it is itself a superkey.
The primary key is the one candidate key we pick, signified by {{c1::underlining}} it; it may be {{c2::composite}} (two or more attributes).

fields.Back: An attribute or set of attributes in one relation that matches the candidate key of some other (possibly the same) relation.

fields.Text: A {{c1::superkey}} is any attribute set that makes tuples unique; a {{c2::candidate key}} is a minimal superkey; the {{c3::primary key}} is the chosen candidate key; a {{c4::foreign key}} matches the candidate key of another (or the same) relation.

fields.Front: Give a set of attributes that is a superkey but NOT a candidate key of the Attribute1/2/3 table.
fields.Back: (Attribute1, Attribute2, Attribute3): removing Attribute3 still leaves a superkey, so it is not minimal.

fields.Front: Department(DeptID, DeptName, MgrEmpID, MgrStartDate) and Employee(EmpID, LastName, FirstName, DeptID, Sex): what are the foreign keys?
fields.Back: Employee.DeptID references Department.DeptID; Department.MgrEmpID references Employee.EmpID.

fields.Front: Car table (LicenseNum, EngineSerialNum, Make, Model, Year): give 3 superkeys.
fields.Back: LicenseNum; EngineSerialNum; and a combination such as (LicenseNum, Make) or (EngineSerialNum, Make). Any set containing either candidate key is a superkey; Make alone is not, because Make repeats.

fields.Text: For the car table the candidate keys are {{c1::LicenseNum}} and {{c2::EngineSerialNum}}; the slide chooses {{c3::EngineSerialNum}} as primary key, though the instructor says the choice depends on what the table is for.

fields.Front: Why is (Make, Model, Year) not a key of the car table?

fields.Back: Keys must be unique; the primary key must be non-null (the entity integrity constraint). Most DBMSs enforce both.

fields.Text: The rule that the primary key must be non-null is called the {{c1::entity integrity constraint}}.

fields.Front: Key constraints and domain constraints apply to what scope? What kind of constraint applies between tables?
fields.Back: To individual (single) tables; referential integrity constraints apply to relationships between tables.

fields.Text: On the course slides, foreign keys are marked with {{c1::an asterisk}} in the column heading.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's plain-language definition of a key.
fields.Back: An attribute, or more than one attribute, that forces each row to be unique, just like your student number.

fields.Text: Keys video objectives: explain the importance of a key; identify key attributes in a table; tell if {{c1::inserting a new row}} will cause a key to fail; know the terms {{c2::primary, foreign, candidate and super}} key.

fields.Front: In Codd's relational model, why is the LastName/FirstName table with two identical Simpson Homer rows not even allowed?
fields.Back: Because no two rows in a relation may be identical; the table has no working key at all.

fields.Front: How does the instructor describe choosing between LicenseNum and EngineSerialNum as the car table's primary key?
fields.Back: It depends on context: to track who drives which car, use LicenseNum; a mechanic or dealer would use EngineSerialNum. The designer decides what the table is for.

fields.Text: The primary key is {{c1::always a candidate key}}: a minimal set of attributes that the database designer picks to identify rows from then on.

fields.Front: What does a DBMS do if you try to store a null primary key or a duplicate primary key?
fields.Back: It refuses. DBMSs enforce both uniqueness and NOT NULL automatically, as long as you have identified the primary key.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's phrasing for what makes a superkey a candidate key.
fields.Back: 'I don't include any extra attributes; I just include the minimum number of attributes that will force uniqueness.' Attribute3 was not needed alongside Attribute1 and Attribute2, so all three form a superkey but not a candidate key.

fields.Front: How does the instructor describe a foreign key in plain words?
fields.Back: An attribute inside a table that references the primary key from another table, e.g. DeptID 11 in Employee refers to DeptID 11 in Department.
